message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
The study proposes a district-wide weekly food waste collection from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot in 4,000 households. It projects a net cost of about £490,000 a year, which it says the provisional £520,000 new-burdens allocation would fully cover.

The cost arithmetic is correct. But the projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce. The study describes flats' participation as "broadly similar" when it was a third of houses'. And projected tonnage exceeds Brookfield's contracted capacity. Corrected, the net cost roughly matches the funding with no headroom, before allowing for treating the excess tonnage elsewhere.

## 1. What checks out

- **Table 1 rates are correct:** 2,112 / 3,200 = 66%, 168 / 800 = 21%, 2,280 / 4,000 = 57%.
- **Table 2 is correct:**
  - Vehicles: 6 × £165,000 = £990,000, ÷ 7 years = £141,400.
  - Crews: 12 operatives × £34,000 = £408,000.
  - Total: £733,400.
- **The projection's own arithmetic is correct:** 52,000 × 64% × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks ≈ 3,290 tonnes. Likewise £74 × 3,290 ≈ £243,000, and £733,400 − £243,000 ≈ £490,000.
- **The pilot mix matches the district.** Both are 20% flats, so the pilot's overall figures can be applied directly.

## 2. Flats' participation was not "broadly similar"

Houses participated at **66%**, flats at **21%**, and flats who took part produced less food waste (1.4 kg against 1.9 kg).

This gap is the pilot's clearest finding, and it points the opposite way from the study's conclusion. Flats make up about 10,400 households across the district, so they need a different approach. That usually means communal bins, different collection points, and targeted communications. The study's claim that a "single, simple service" will work across all housing types isn't supported by its own data.

## 3. The projection uses 64% participation; the pilot shows 57%

The 64% figure doesn't appear in the pilot data. Because the pilot's housing mix matches the district's, the pilot's own figures apply directly. Its average yield per participating household is also slightly lower than stated: (2,112 × 1.9 + 168 × 1.4) ÷ 2,280 = 1.86 kg, not 1.9.

| | As stated | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| Participation | 64% | 57% |
| Kg per participating household | 1.9 | 1.86 |
| **Annual tonnage** | **3,290 t** | **~2,870 t** |
| Disposal saving (× £74/t) | £243,000 | ~£212,000 |
| **Net annual cost** | **£490,000** | **~£521,000** |

Projecting houses and flats separately gives the same corrected total, about 2,870 t.

At about £521,000, the net cost is slightly above the £520,000 allocation, not "fully covered" with £30,000 to spare.

## 4. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes

Brookfield has offered **1,800 t a year** until its expansion in 2029. Even the corrected tonnage of about 2,870 t exceeds that by roughly **1,070 t**. On the study's own projection, the excess is nearly 1,500 t.

- The study applies Brookfield's £38 gate fee to every tonne. The excess would have to go to the next plant, **46 miles away**, at an unknown gate fee plus haulage costs. That makes the saving per tonne on the excess smaller, and possibly negative.
- "Treatment is local", as the author describes it, is true for only about 60% of the tonnage, and only until 2029.

With the excess costed, the net cost will exceed the funding allocation.

## 5. Missing or unclear costs

The author's summary says "every cost line is shown", but several are missing or unclear:

- **On-costs for crews.** If £34,000 is the operatives' salary alone, employer pension and National Insurance contributions add roughly a quarter or more.
- **Cover.** There is no allowance for spare vehicles or relief crew to cover breakdowns, holidays and sickness.
- **One-off and support costs.** Recruitment, training, the dedicated phone line and web page (section 6), supervision and depot space aren't in Table 2.
- **Capital.** The £990,000 vehicle purchase has to be paid when the vehicles are ordered and delivered, in 2026/27. Depreciation spreads the cost on paper but doesn't fund the purchase. The study should state whether the new-burdens funding covers capital or only running costs.
- **Incineration contract.** Confirm that diverting waste actually saves £112 a tonne. Some incineration contracts commit the council to a minimum tonnage, which would reduce the saving.
- **The £520,000 is provisional.** "Fully funded" should be stated as conditional on that allocation being confirmed.

## 6. Smaller points

- **The survey.** The 81% satisfaction figure has no response rate. Participating households are probably over-represented among respondents.
- **The pilot may flatter long-run participation.** It covered January to June, and new schemes often attract early enthusiasm. A whole-year and post-launch tracking plan would help.
- **Rollout logistics.** Delivering caddies to 52,000 households in March is a big job, and the timetable doesn't say when caddies will be procured. Recruiting from February and training in March is tight.
- **A possible upside the study doesn't count.** Lower residual bin weight might allow residual collection rounds to be reorganised.

## How the author's description compares

| Author's claim | Holds? |
|---|---|
| Projections based on how residents actually behave | No. They use 64% participation; the pilot shows 57% |
| Participation held up across houses and flats | No. 66% for houses against 21% for flats |
| A single, simple service across the district | Not supported; flats need a different approach |
| Every cost line is shown | No. Cover, on-costs, recruitment, training, phone line and capital funding are missing or unclear |
| Disposal saving uses actual costs | The rates are actual, but they are applied to more tonnage than Brookfield can take |
| Net cost of £490,000, fully covered | About £521,000 on corrected tonnage, before treating the excess elsewhere; the funding is provisional |
| Treatment is local | Only for 1,800 t a year, until 2029 |
| Timetable works back from vehicle lead time | Yes, though caddy procurement and recruitment are tight |

## Recommendation

**The service is statutory, so the question is how to deliver it, not whether.** Before Cabinet approves:

1. **Redo the projection** at 57% participation, or project houses and flats separately. About 2,870 t is the realistic base.
2. **Cost the tonnage above 1,800 t** at the 46-mile plant, or negotiate extra capacity with Brookfield before 2029.
3. **Design a separate approach for flats**, and set a participation target for them.
4. **Complete Table 2.** Add on-costs, cover, one-off costs and the phone line, and set out how the £990,000 vehicle purchase will be funded.
5. **Present the funding position honestly.** On the corrected figures the net cost is roughly equal to or above the provisional allocation. Cabinet should know that before committing.

The vehicle order deadline is real, so it's reasonable to authorise the vehicle order now, on the condition that the revised financial case comes back to Cabinet before the service launches.
